claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The ATPase activity of ΔG2(WT) was barely stimulated by adding dsDNA.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the ATPase activity of ΔG2(WT) was barely stimulated by adding dsDNA.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The introduction of SMC-TR mutations greatly reduced the ATPase activities of both the holocomplex and ΔG2 subcomplex.
claims.source: The introduction of SMC-TR mutations greatly reduced the ATPase activities of both the holocomplex and ΔG2 subcomplex.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: CAP-G2 negatively regulates the ATPase activity of condensin II.
claims.source: Taken together, these results demonstrated that CAP-G2 negatively regulates the ATPase activity of condensin II as well as its ability to associate with chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing increased ATPase activity upon CAP-G2 deletion.

claims.claim: CAP-G2 negatively regulates condensin II's ability to associate with chromosomes.
claims.source: Taken together, these results demonstrated that CAP-G2 negatively regulates the ATPase activity of condensin II as well as its ability to associate with chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing increased chromosome association upon CAP-G2 deletion.

claims.claim: Human CAP-D3 is a polypeptide with 1498 amino acids.
claims.source: Human CAP-D3 is a polypeptide with 1498 amino acids, in which a HEAT-repeat-rich section is followed by a C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) of around 200 amino-acid long (Figure 4A; Ono et al., 2003; Yoshimura and Hirano, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The CAP-D3 C-terminal IDR contains as many as 11 Cdk1 consensus (S/TP) sites.
claims.source: Notably, the C-terminal IDR domain, which we refer to as the C-tail in the current study, contains as many as 11 Cdk1 consensus (S/TP) sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Mitosis-specific phosphorylation in the CAP-D3 C-tail regulates condensin II functions.
claims.source: Previous studies reported that mitosis-specific phosphorylation in the CAP-D3 C-tail regulates condensin II functions (Abe et al., 2011; Bakhrebah et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The full-length CAP-D3 (D3-FL), but not the C-terminally truncated version of CAP-D3 (D3-dC), underwent progressive, electrophoretic mobility shifts when incubated in metaphase extracts.
claims.source: When holo(WT) and holo(D3-dC) were incubated in metaphase extracts, the full-length CAP-D3 (D3-FL), but not the C-terminally truncated version of CAP-D3 (D3-dC), underwent progressive, electrophoretic mobility shifts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail removed most, if not all, of the mitosis-specific phosphorylation sites.
claims.source: A pair of phosphospecific antibodies against pT1415 and pS1474 recognized shifted D3-FL, but not D3-dC, suggesting that the deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail removed most, if not all, of the mitosis-specific phosphorylation sites.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using phospho-specific antibodies shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The ATPase activity of holo(D3-dC) was significantly higher than that of holo(WT) either in the presence or absence of dsDNA.
claims.source: In the ATPase assay, we found that the ATPase activity of holo(D3-dC) was significantly higher than that of holo(WT) either in the presence or absence of dsDNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Higher levels of chromosome association were observed with holo(D3-dC) than with holo(WT) at all concentrations tested (25, 50, and 200 nM).
claims.source: In the add-back assay, higher levels of chromosome association were observed with holo(D3-dC) than with holo(WT) at all concentrations tested (25, 50, and 200 nM; Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The chromosome structure formed by holo(D3-dC) at 200 nM was no longer chenille-like: DAPI signals were more confined toward the axis positive for hCAP-H2.
claims.source: Remarkably, we noticed that the chromosome structure formed by holo(D3-dC) at 200 nM was no longer chenille-like: DAPI signals were more confined toward the axis positive for hCAP-H2 (Figure 4C, left, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), being compacted laterally into structures reminiscent of rod-shaped chromosomes produced by condensin I (Kinoshita et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: When the concentration of holo(D3-dC) was lowered to 50 nM, its chromosome association was reduced to a level similar to that of holo(WT) at 200 nM addition and formed similar chenille-like chromosomes.
claims.source: However, when the concentration of holo(D3-dC) was lowered to 50 nM, its chromosome association was reduced to a level similar to that of holo(WT) at 200 nM addition and formed similar chenille-like chromosomes (Figure 4C, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The CAP-D3 C-tail negatively regulates condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly.
claims.source: These results demonstrated that the CAP-D3 C-tail negatively regulates condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly, and further implicated that a high level of chromosome association of holo(D3-dC) supports the conversion from chenille-like to laterally compacted rod-like structures.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of CAP-D3 C-tail deletion.

claims.claim: A high level of chromosome association of holo(D3-dC) supports the conversion from chenille-like to laterally compacted rod-like structures.
claims.source: These results demonstrated that the CAP-D3 C-tail negatively regulates condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly, and further implicated that a high level of chromosome association of holo(D3-dC) supports the conversion from chenille-like to laterally compacted rod-like structures.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing dose-dependent effects.

claims.claim: Slightly higher levels of chromosome association were observed with ΔG2(D3-dC) than with ΔG2(WT).
claims.source: We found that slightly higher levels of chromosome association were observed with ΔG2(D3-dC) than with ΔG2(WT) (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The chromosomes formed by ΔG2(D3-dC) were chenille-like rather than rod-like, even at the highest concentration of 200 nM.
claims.source: Importantly, however, the chromosomes formed by ΔG2(D3-dC), unlike those formed by holo(D3-dC), were chenille-like rather than rod-like, even at the highest concentration of 200 nM (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claims.claim: CAP-G2 has a rather cryptic role in chromosome shaping, which can only be uncovered when the holocomplex is overloaded on chromosomes by deleting the CAP-D3 C-tail.
claims.source: These results showed that CAP-G2 has a rather cryptic role in chromosome shaping, which can only be uncovered when the holocomplex is overloaded on chromosomes by deleting the CAP-D3 C-tail.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing holo(D3-dC) and ΔG2(D3-dC).

claims.claim: Two basic amino acid clusters (BC1 and BC2) conserved in the central region of Brn1/CAP-H form part of a unique DNA-binding subdomain ('safety belt').
claims.source: A previous study using budding yeast condensin had reported that two basic amino acid clusters (BC1 and BC2) conserved in the central region of Brn1/CAP-H form part of a unique DNA-binding subdomain ('safety belt'; Kschonsak et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claims.claim: BC1/2 mutations in human CAP-H caused hypomorphic defects in condensin I-mediated chromosome assembly in Xenopus egg extract.
claims.source: It had also been shown that BC1/2 mutations (substitutions of all basic residues with aspartic acids) in human CAP-H caused hypomorphic defects in condensin I-mediated chromosome assembly in Xenopus egg extract (Kinoshita et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The BC1D or BC2D mutations caused partial defects in chromosome association of condensin II, resulting in the formation of discontinuous axes.
claims.source: We found that the BC1D or BC2D mutations caused partial defects in chromosome association of condensin II, resulting in the formation of discontinuous axes (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: Holo(H2-BC1/2D), a holocomplex harboring both BC1D and BC2D mutations, failed to associate with chromatin, leaving a cloud-like morphology.
claims.source: In contrast, holo(H2-BC1/2D), a holocomplex harboring both BC1D and BC2D mutations, failed to associate with chromatin, leaving a cloud-like morphology.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: The two sets of BC mutations caused synergistic defects in condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly.
claims.source: Thus, the two sets of mutations caused synergistic defects in condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing single and double mutants.

claims.claim: Deletion of CAP-G2 from mutant complexes harboring BC1D, BC2D, or BC1/2D partially rescued their defects in chromosome association and axis formation.
claims.source: Interestingly, deletion of CAP-G2 from these mutant complexes harboring BC1D, BC2D, or BC1/2D partially rescued their defects in chromosome association and axis formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the BC1/2D mutations do not cause complete loss of condensin II functions when the negative regulation by CAP-G2 is eliminated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The BC1/2D mutations do not cause complete loss of condensin II functions when the negative regulation by CAP-G2 is eliminated.
claims.source: Interestingly, deletion of CAP-G2 from these mutant complexes harboring BC1D, BC2D, or BC1/2D partially rescued their defects in chromosome association and axis formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the BC1/2D mutations do not cause complete loss of condensin II functions when the negative regulation by CAP-G2 is eliminated.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing partial rescue.

claims.claim: Condensin II holo(WT) displayed a weak ATP-stimulated binding and caused compaction of the banana-shaped chromatin in an ATP-dependent manner.
claims.source: We found that condensin II holo(WT) displayed a weak ATP-stimulated binding and caused compaction of the banana-shaped chromatin in an ATP-dependent manner (Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the extract-free assay shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: Neither ATP-stimulated binding nor ATP-dependent compaction was observed when the ATP-hydrolysis-deficient holo(SMC-TR) was added.
claims.source: Neither ATP-stimulated binding nor ATP-dependent compaction was observed when the ATP-hydrolysis-deficient holo(SMC-TR) was added.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the extract-free assay shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: ΔD3(WT) and ΔD3ΔG2(WT) were barely detectable on the chromatin in either the absence or presence of ATP in the extract-free assay.
claims.source: ΔD3(WT) and ΔD3ΔG2(WT) were barely detectable on the chromatin in either the absence or presence of ATP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the extract-free assay shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: ΔG2(WT) displayed much greater activities of both ATP-stimulated binding and ATP-dependent compaction than holo(WT) in the extract-free assay.
claims.source: Strikingly, ΔG2(WT) displayed much greater activities of both ATP-stimulated binding and ATP-dependent compaction than holo(WT).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the extract-free assay shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: The CAP-D3 C-tail lacking holo(D3-dC) displayed higher activities than holo(WT) in the extract-free assay.
claims.source: The CAP-D3 C-tail lacking holo(D3-dC) was also tested and was found to display higher activities than holo(WT) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the extract-free assay shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The swollen chromatin binding assay allows probing for ATP-stimulated chromatin binding and ATP-dependent chromatin compaction by condensin II under an extract-free condition.
claims.source: Thus, the swollen chromatin binding assay allows us to probe for ATP-stimulated chromatin binding and ATP-dependent chromatin compaction by condensin II under an extract-free condition.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results of the extract-free assay.

claims.claim: The simple extract-free assay could recapitulate, at least in part, the differences in chromatin binding between the wild-type and the mutant complexes observed in Xenopus egg extracts.
claims.source: Importantly, this simple assay could recapitulate, at least in part, the differences in chromatin binding between the wild-type and the mutant complexes observed in Xenopus egg extracts.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of results from extract-based and extract-free assays.

claims.claim: In condensin I, the two HEAT subunits, CAP-D2 and CAP-G, have antagonistic functions in the dynamic assembly of chromosome axes.
claims.source: A previous study from our laboratory had demonstrated that a pair of HEAT subunits of condensin I, CAP-D2, and CAP-G, have antagonistic functions in the dynamic assembly of chromosome axes (Kinoshita et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Deletion of CAP-G decreased chromosome association of condensin I and caused the formation of a chromosome structure with fuzzy surfaces and abnormally thin axes.
claims.source: Deletion of CAP-G decreased chromosome association of condensin I and caused the formation of a chromosome structure with fuzzy surfaces and abnormally thin axes.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge from previous studies on condensin I.

claims.claim: The essential requirement of CAP-D3 in condensin II-mediated axis formation was parallel to the requirements of CAP-D2 in condensin I-mediated axis formation.
claims.source: Although the essential requirement of CAP-D3 in condensin II-mediated axis formation was parallel to the requirements of CAP-D2 in condensin I-mediated axis formation (Kinoshita et al., 2015; Kinoshita et al., 2022), we were surprised to find that CAP-G2 has a very strong negative impact on condensin II functions.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous studies on condensin I.

claims.claim: The balancing acts of the two HEAT subunits, originally proposed for condensin I, also operate in condensin II, but such actions are fine-tuned differently in each complex.
claims.source: We suggest that the balancing acts of the two HEAT subunits, originally proposed for condensin I (Kinoshita et al., 2015), also operate in condensin II, but that such actions are fine-tuned differently in each complex (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing condensins I and II.

claims.claim: In condensin II, CAP-D3-driven axis assembly is intrinsically dominant, which is counter-balanced by the strong suppressive action of CAP-G2.
claims.source: In the case of condensin II, for example, CAP-D3-driven axis assembly is intrinsically dominant, which is counter-balanced by the strong suppressive action of CAP-G2.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data on condensin II.

claims.claim: Deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail from the condensin I holocomplex causes no noticeable impact on mitotic chromosome assembly in Xenopus egg extracts.
claims.source: This mode of regulation is unique to condensin II, because deletion of the CAP-D2 C-tail from the condensin I holocomplex causes no noticeable impact on mitotic chromosome assembly in Xenopus egg extracts (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; Kinoshita et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and citation.

claims.claim: Deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail has a greater impact on the holocomplex than on the ΔG2 subcomplex.
claims.source: The observation that deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail has a greater impact on the holocomplex than on the ΔG2 subcomplex (Figure 4) suggests an overlap in the negative regulatory roles of CAP-G2 and the CAP-D3 C-tail (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: There is an overlap in the negative regulatory roles of CAP-G2 and the CAP-D3 C-tail.
claims.source: The observation that deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail has a greater impact on the holocomplex than on the ΔG2 subcomplex (Figure 4) suggests an overlap in the negative regulatory roles of CAP-G2 and the CAP-D3 C-tail (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing effects of deletions.

claims.claim: A recent study using cross-linking mass spectrometry has revealed physical contacts between an N-terminal region of CAP-G2 and a C-terminal region of CAP-D3.
claims.source: A recent study using cross-linking mass spectrometry has revealed physical contacts between an N-terminal region of CAP-G2 and a C-terminal region of CAP-D3 (Kong et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: CAP-G2 may interfere with the action of CAP-D3 by directly interacting with the CAP-D3 C-tail.
claims.source: It is therefore possible that CAP-G2 interferes with the action of CAP-D3 by directly interacting with the CAP-D3 C-tail.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from structural data.

claims.claim: Mitosis-specific phosphorylation by Cdk1 of the CAP-D3 C-tail may destabilize the suppressing interaction with CAP-G2, thereby activating CAP-D3-mediated axis assembly.
claims.source: Future experiments should test the hypothesis that mitosis-specific phosphorylation by Cdk1 of the CAP-D3 C-tail destabilizes the suppressing interaction, thereby activating CAP-D3-mediated axis assembly.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a hypothesis for future testing.

claims.claim: The chromosome structure produced in Xenopus egg extract by holo(D3-dC) is qualitatively different from that produced by ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC).
claims.source: Despite the potential functional crosstalk between CAP-G2 and the CAP-D3 C-tail, it is important to note that the chromosome structure produced in Xenopus egg extract by holo(D3-dC) is qualitatively different from that produced by ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing chromosome morphologies.

claims.claim: ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC) accumulate at the axis of chromosomes in a dose-dependent manner, but such accumulation does not cause enrichment of DNA at the axis.
claims.source: While ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC) accumulate at the axis of chromosomes in a dose-dependent manner, such accumulation does not cause enrichment of DNA at the axis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claims.claim: ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC) shift the chromosomal DNA to elongate the overall axis while keeping their chenille-like morphology under high-dose conditions.
claims.source: Instead, ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC) shift the chromosomal DNA to elongate the overall axis while keeping their chenille-like morphology under high-dose conditions (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Holo(D3-dC) increases the DNA level at the axial region under a high-dose condition and produces rod-like chromosomes rather than chenille-like chromosomes.
claims.source: In contrast, holo(D3-dC) increases the DNA level at the axial region under a high-dose condition and produces rod-like chromosomes rather than chenille-like chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: CAP-G2 is not a mere inhibitor but has a rather cryptic function in the compaction of non-axial bulk chromatin.
claims.source: These observations suggest that CAP-G2 is not a mere inhibitor but has a rather cryptic function in the compaction of non-axial bulk chromatin (Figure 7A, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing different mutants.

claims.claim: The function of CAP-G2 in bulk chromatin compaction is observed only when the holocomplex is overloaded on chromosomes by deleting the CAP-D3 C-tail.
claims.source: However, this function of CAP-G2 is observed only when the holocomplex is overloaded on chromosomes by deleting the CAP-D3 C-tail.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claims.claim: Holo(D3-dC), but not ΔG2(WT), retains DNA-stimulated ATPase activity.
claims.source: Intriguingly, we find that holo(D3-dC), but not ΔG2(WT), retains DNA-stimulated ATPase activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays.

claims.claim: ATP binding and hydrolysis by the SMC subunits are essential for the functions of condensin I in Xenopus egg extracts.
claims.source: Our previous work demonstrated that ATP binding and hydrolysis by the SMC subunits are essential for the functions of condensin I in Xenopus egg extracts (Kinoshita et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The SMC ATPase cycle is essential for the functions of condensin II.
claims.source: Thus, the SMC ATPase cycle is essential for the functions of condensin II, too, even in the absence of its inhibitory subunit CAP-G2.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data with SMC-TR mutants.

claims.claim: Two basic patches (BC1 and BC2) present in the central region of budding yeast Brn1/CAP-H, together with Ycg1/CAP-G, have been proposed to form a unique DNA-binding region, referred to as the 'safety belt'.
claims.source: Two basic patches (BC1 and BC2) present in the central region of budding yeast Brn1/CAP-H, together with Ycg1/CAP-G, have been proposed to form a unique DNA-binding region, referred to as the 'safety belt' (Kschonsak et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claims.claim: The BC1/2D mutations in the CAP-H2 subunit of mammalian condensin II completely abolish its ability to associate with chromatin.
claims.source: In contrast, our current results show that the BC1/2D mutations in the CAP-H2 subunit of mammalian condensin II completely abolish its ability to associate with chromatin (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: There has been no direct evidence to date that mammalian condensins use a safety-belt mechanism for DNA binding as demonstrated by budding yeast condensin.
claims.source: Although the phenotypic differences observed between condensins I and II are intriguing, it should be noted that there has been no direct evidence to date that mammalian condensins use a safety-belt mechanism for DNA binding as demonstrated by budding yeast condensin.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the current state of the field.

claims.claim: The functional requirement for CAP-G2 may be somewhat relaxed in condensin from the filamentous fungus Chaetomium thermophilum.
claims.source: Even if a similar mechanism operates in mammalian condensin II, it is possible that the functional requirement for CAP-G2 is somewhat relaxed, as has been recently shown in condensin from the filamentous fungus Chaetomium thermophilum (Shaltiel et al., 2022).

results.result: Recombinant mammalian condensin II holocomplex functionally replaces endogenous condensin II in Xenopus egg extracts depleted of both condensins I and II, enabling assembly of chenille-like chromosomes with internal axes at 200 nM concentration.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 and C117-C120 collectively demonstrate that recombinant condensin II holo(WT) at 200 nM restores chromosome assembly in Δcond I/II extracts, producing structures similar to endogenous condensin II. The data in Figures 1B-E provide clear visual and quantitative evidence, though the required concentration (200 nM) is ~8-fold higher than endogenous levels (~25 nM), which the authors acknowledge and attribute to species differences or post-translational modifications.

results.result: CAP-D3 is essential for condensin II-mediated chromosome axis assembly, as deletion of CAP-D3 prevents axis formation and greatly reduces chromatin association.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C30, C34, and C36 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figures 2A-B showing that ΔD3(WT) and ΔD3ΔG2(WT) fail to form DAPI-dense axes and display weak chromatin association. This parallels the essential role of CAP-D2 in condensin I (C78), providing consistent evidence for CAP-D3's positive role in axis formation.

results.result: CAP-G2 negatively regulates condensin II chromosome association and axis assembly, as deletion of CAP-G2 greatly increases chromosome association and allows axis formation at 8-fold lower concentration (25 nM vs 200 nM).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C31-C33, C35, C37, and C121 are well-supported by data in Figures 2A-D showing that ΔG2(WT) produces chenille-like chromosomes with extremely high hCAP-H2 accumulation at axes, and that 25 nM ΔG2(WT) produces comparable structures to 200 nM holo(WT). Time-course data (Figure 2—supplement 1C) further demonstrates earlier chromatin association for ΔG2(WT). This represents a major mechanistic finding distinguishing condensin II from condensin I.

results.result: The SMC ATPase cycle is essential for condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly, as ATP hydrolysis-deficient SMC-TR mutations abolish axis formation even in the absence of CAP-G2.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C38-C41, C94-C95 are supported by data in Figure 3A-B showing that both holo(SMC-TR) and ΔG2(SMC-TR) fail to assemble chromosomes despite some chromatin association by ΔG2(SMC-TR). This parallels previous findings for condensin I (C94) and demonstrates that ATP hydrolysis is required regardless of CAP-G2 presence, establishing it as a fundamental requirement.

results.result: CAP-G2 negatively regulates condensin II ATPase activity, as deletion of CAP-G2 increases basal ATP hydrolysis >3-fold but eliminates DNA-stimulated activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 are supported by ATPase assay data in Figure 3C showing that holo(WT) has modest basal activity that is stimulated 2-fold by DNA, while ΔG2(WT) has >3-fold higher basal activity but no DNA stimulation. SMC-TR mutations reduce activity in both complexes. This biochemical data complements the chromosome assembly results and provides mechanistic insight into CAP-G2's negative regulatory role.

results.result: Deletion of the CAP-D3 C-terminal tail increases condensin II chromosome association and ATPase activity, and at high concentration (200 nM) converts chenille-like chromosomes to laterally compacted rod-like structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C53-C58 are supported by data in Figures 4B-C and Figure 4—supplement 1C showing that holo(D3-dC) has higher ATPase activity and chromosome association than holo(WT), and produces rod-like rather than chenille-like chromosomes at 200 nM. At 50 nM, holo(D3-dC) produces chenille-like chromosomes similar to 200 nM holo(WT), demonstrating dose-dependent effects. This reveals a unique negative regulatory mechanism specific to condensin II.

results.result: CAP-G2 has a cryptic function in lateral chromatin compaction that is only revealed when the holocomplex is overloaded on chromosomes by deleting the CAP-D3 C-tail, as holo(D3-dC) produces rod-like chromosomes while ΔG2(D3-dC) maintains chenille-like morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C59-C61, C87-C92 are supported by data in Figures 4D and Figure 4—supplement 2B-C showing that ΔG2(D3-dC) produces chenille-like chromosomes even at 200 nM, unlike holo(D3-dC) which produces rod-like chromosomes. The line scan profiles demonstrate that ΔG2 complexes elongate axes without enriching DNA at the axis, while holo(D3-dC) increases axial DNA levels. This reveals CAP-G2's hidden positive function in bulk chromatin compaction.

results.result: Basic amino acid clusters (BC1 and BC2) in CAP-H2 are essential for condensin II chromosome association, with BC1/2D double mutations completely abolishing chromatin binding while single mutations cause partial defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C62-C66, C98 are supported by data in Figure 5B-C showing that BC1D or BC2D single mutations cause partial defects with discontinuous axes, while BC1/2D double mutations completely prevent chromatin association. This demonstrates synergistic effects and contrasts with the hypomorphic phenotype of BC1/2D mutations in condensin I (C63), revealing functional differences between the two complexes.

results.result: Deletion of CAP-G2 partially rescues the chromosome association defects of BC1/2D mutants, suggesting an alternative CAP-D3-dependent loading pathway that operates in the absence of CAP-G2.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 and C101-C102 are supported by data in Figure 5—supplement 1 showing that ΔG2(H2-BC1/2D) retains some chromatin association ability while holo(H2-BC1/2D) does not. However, the proposed CAP-D3-dependent loading pathway (C102) is speculative and requires further experimental validation. The rescue is only partial, and the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: An extract-free swollen chromatin binding assay recapitulates ATP-stimulated chromatin binding and compaction by condensin II, with ΔG2(WT) showing much greater activity than holo(WT) and SMC-TR mutations abolishing activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C75 and C106 are supported by data in Figures 6A-B and Figure 6—supplement 1 showing that the extract-free assay reproduces key differences between wild-type and mutant complexes observed in egg extracts. Holo(WT) shows weak ATP-dependent binding and compaction, ΔG2(WT) shows much stronger activity, ΔD3 complexes show minimal activity, and SMC-TR mutations abolish activity. This validates the assay as a simplified system for studying condensin II function.

results.result: The CAP-D3 C-terminal tail contains 11 Cdk1 consensus sites that undergo mitosis-specific phosphorylation in egg extracts, as demonstrated by electrophoretic mobility shifts and phospho-specific antibodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by sequence analysis (Figure 4—supplement 1A) and experimental data (Figure 4—supplement 1B) showing that full-length CAP-D3 undergoes progressive mobility shifts in metaphase extracts that are recognized by phospho-specific antibodies against pT1415 and pS1474, while the C-tail deletion mutant does not. This establishes the C-tail as a target for mitotic regulation.

results.result: The balancing acts of HEAT subunits operate in both condensin I and II but are fine-tuned differently, with CAP-D3-driven axis assembly being intrinsically dominant in condensin II and counter-balanced by strong CAP-G2 suppression.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 synthesize the experimental findings into a comparative model. The claims are supported by the collective data showing that while both condensins have antagonistic HEAT subunits (C76), condensin II shows much stronger negative regulation by CAP-G2 compared to CAP-G in condensin I. The model is well-supported by the experimental evidence, though it represents an interpretive framework rather than direct experimental observation.

results.result: The CAP-D3 C-tail's negative regulatory role is unique to condensin II, as deletion of the CAP-D2 C-tail in condensin I has no effect on chromosome assembly, and there is functional overlap between CAP-G2 and the CAP-D3 C-tail.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 are supported by data in Figure 4—supplement 3 showing that condensin I holo(D2-dC) produces normal rod-shaped chromosomes identical to holo(WT), and by Figure 4 showing that CAP-D3 C-tail deletion has greater impact on the holocomplex than on ΔG2 subcomplex. This establishes a condensin II-specific regulatory mechanism and suggests functional overlap between two negative regulators.

results.result: CAP-G2 may interfere with CAP-D3 function through direct interaction with the CAP-D3 C-tail, with mitosis-specific Cdk1 phosphorylation potentially destabilizing this interaction to activate axis assembly.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 is supported by citation to cross-linking mass spectrometry data showing physical contacts between CAP-G2 N-terminus and CAP-D3 C-terminus. However, claims C85-C86 are explicitly speculative (marked as "SPECULATION" in evidence_type) and proposed as hypotheses for future testing. The mechanistic model lacks direct experimental validation in the current study.

results.result: Holo(D3-dC) retains DNA-stimulated ATPase activity while ΔG2(WT) does not, suggesting mechanistic differences between the two mutant complexes.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 is supported by ATPase assay data in Figure 3C and Figure 4—supplement 1C showing that holo(D3-dC) maintains DNA-stimulated activity (though at higher basal level) while ΔG2(WT) has high basal activity but no DNA stimulation. This biochemical difference correlates with the distinct chromosome morphologies produced by these complexes and provides mechanistic insight.

results.result: Condensin II can function largely without CAP-G2, providing an evolutionary explanation for frequent loss of the cap-g2 gene during insect evolution while cap-d3 and cap-h2 are retained.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113 connect the experimental findings to evolutionary observations. The functional data showing that ΔG2 complexes can assemble chromosomes (C113) is well-supported. The evolutionary claims (C108-C112) are supported by citations to previous studies documenting condensin II distribution and gene loss patterns across species. The synthesis provides a compelling evolutionary framework, though the connection is correlative rather than causative.

results.result: Background context on condensin I and II localization, functions, and species distribution in mitotic chromosome assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C22 provide established background knowledge about condensin complexes, supported by multiple citations to previous studies. These claims accurately represent the current understanding of condensin biology and provide necessary context for the experimental work. All claims are appropriately cited and consistent with the literature.

results.result: Background context on condensin mechanisms including loop extrusion, DNA translocation, safety belt structure, and gaps in current understanding.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25, C96, C99-C100, C103-C105, C114-C116 provide background on condensin mechanisms and current challenges in the field. All claims are appropriately cited to previous studies. Claim C116 is speculative but clearly presented as the authors' suspicion. These claims establish the rationale for the current study and identify gaps in knowledge that the work addresses.

results.result: A fraction of recombinant hCAP-H2 is phosphorylated when expressed in insect cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 is supported by phosphatase treatment data in Figure 1—supplement 1E showing that one of two hCAP-H2 bands migrates faster after phosphatase treatment. This is a technical observation about the recombinant protein preparation that may be relevant for interpreting functional assays.
